title: Independence Test for Linear Non-Gaussian Data and Applications in Causal Discovery
claim: Dependence can hide in conditional structure: constant conditional mean and variance accompany independence, while their variation signals dependence, even when scatter plots look similar.

The top row shows blue scatter plots of Y against X: a parabola-like cloud, six vertical strips at discrete X values, and two diffuse linear clouds that look similar. The bottom row shows the conditional density P(Y|X) for each X bin as blue filled violin-like shapes. Dashed black and red lines overlay the conditional mean E[Y|X] and the conditional variance Var(Y|X). In case I the mean curves and the variance is nearly flat. In case II the mean and variance are both flat although the densities change shape. In case III the mean rises with X while the variance stays flat. In case IV both lines are flat. abstract: Independence testing involves determining whether two variables are independent based on observed samples, which is a fundamental problem in statistics and machine learning. Existing testing methods, such as HSIC, can theoretically detect broad forms of dependence, but may sacrifice statistical power when applied to limited samples with background knowledge of the distribution. In this paper, we focus on the linear non-Gaussian data, a widely supported model in scientific data analysis and causal discovery, where variables are linked linearly with noise terms that are non-Gaussian distributed. We provide a new theoretical characterization of independence in this case, showing that constancy of the conditional mean and variance is sufficient to guarantee independence under linear non-Gaussian models. Building on this result, we develop a kernel-based testing framework with provable asymptotic guarantees. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves higher power than existing approaches and significantly improves downstream causal discovery performance.
